topics.title: [RFC & Research] Automated Channel Liquidity Rebalancing on Fiber Network

recent_posts.topic_title: [RFC & Research] Automated Channel Liquidity Rebalancing on Fiber Network
recent_posts.author: ILE_LABS
recent_posts.content_text:
Following up on this thread.
The post has been moved to Infrastructure, but we have not yet received technical feedback on whether the problem is relevant to current Fiber development.
The prototype targets a specific gap: Fiber supports manual circular rebalancing through build_router, but operators still have to inspect topology, calculate fees, evaluate timelock exposure, and manage channel capacity manually.
Before we invest further, we need to know:
Is automated channel-liquidity rebalancing a current Fiber priority?
Are the existing build_router and self-payment APIs considered sufficient?
Would a read-only safety and route-analysis tool be useful to Fiber node operators?
Is there an existing tool or planned implementation that already addresses this?
If this is already planned, or not a current priority, i will need an update on that directly so we can move forward. If it is relevant, we would appreciate guidance. Thank you.

recent_posts.author: xingtianchunyan
recent_posts.content_text:
Hello @FidelCoder,
Thank you for taking the time to revise the proposal. The committee has completed its review and, after careful consideration, regrets to inform you that it has decided to reject the LiquidLane proposal.
We wish to maintain transparency regarding the reasons behind this decision:
The funding security and custody solutions are too rudimentary and fail to address the core risks that concern the committee:
The proposal states that LPs pool funds in an on-chain vault, with LiquidLane using these funds to deploy Fiber channels and returning the funds to the “fixed recovery lock” upon expiration. However, the proposal does not adequately explain how the custody mechanism works in detail, particularly: what happens if the operator disappears during the operation of the channel? How is the recovery lock enforced on the chain? And how can malicious operators be prevented from closing the channel and draining the vault before the recovery process is triggered? These are precisely the issues that the committee has repeatedly emphasized in previous reviews of Fiber custody, and the current description does not provide convincing technical safeguards.We would also like to point out that the DevLaunch Kit precedent establishes a general principle: basic CKB transfers do not require the deployment of contracts; therefore, proposals must explain why a custom contract or vault structure is needed for hosting, rather than relying on existing locking scripts or multi-signature mechanisms.
The design of the custody mechanism contains fundamental contradictions, and the issue of LP trust has not been resolved:
The proposal claims that merchants “cannot access the vault or provider-node, nor do they have any loan balance available for withdrawal” – which means, according to this description, the merchants’ balance starts at zero. But if merchants have no balance, and LiquidLane must forward an equivalent amount through the merchant’s channel for each customer payment, then in reality LiquidLane functions as a centralized intermediary for settlements between incoming and outgoing channels. It is more of a managed exchange hub than a “liquidity layer”.
The committee is concerned that this design concentrates trust in the operators, rather than making use of Fiber’s channel-based security model. Additionally, the proposal supports “specific one-way Fiber channels,” which limits the ability for atomic swaps as well as the overall usability of the Fiber network.
We are extremely grateful for all the hard work your team has put in. Please keep building, and feel free to contact us if you have any questions.
Best regards,
xingtian
On behalf of the Spark Program Committee
cc: @Hanssen @yixiu.ckbfans.bit @zz_tovarishch

topics.title: Spark Program | CKB Revocable Timelock (CRT) — Timelock Encryption You Can Cancel

recent_posts.topic_title: Spark Program | CKB Revocable Timelock (CRT) — Timelock Encryption You Can Cancel
recent_posts.author: xingtianchunyan
recent_posts.content_text:
Hi @psawyerberlin,
Thank you for your continued interest in the Spark Program and for submitting the CKB Revocable Timelock (CRT) proposal.
After review by the Spark Program committee, your proposal has been assigned a status of Pending. This is not a rejection, but an invitation to revise.
The committee recognizes the genuine pain point you’ve identified — the inability to revoke or cancel a timelock encryption once scheduled is a real limitation in drand-based systems, and your use cases (VoteSecure, sealed-bid auctions, dead man’s switches) are well-articulated. The concept of leveraging CKB’s cell consumption and type-id uniqueness as a “kill switch” is creative and aligns well with CKB’s state model.
However, the committee has several concerns that need to be addressed before this can proceed:
Main Revision Recommendations:
Decentralization & Node Participation:
Please disclose the decentralization level of the CRT node network. Who can run a node? Is it permissionless — can anyone participate in key-holding and publishing? If nodes are restricted to a set of operators you select or deploy yourself, the security model changes significantly and you need to clarify this explicitly. Please detail the node discovery mechanism, incentive structure (if any), and how you prevent a malicious node from refusing to publish or colluding with other nodes.
The “No Delete” Problem — Accountability Mechanism:
Your design states that nodes hold a fresh per-switch private key and should delete it if the owner cancels. But nothing on CKB forces a node to actually delete its copy. A node could keep the private key and decrypt the data later regardless of the on-chain condition, or after the cell is consumed. The committee would like you to explicitly address: if a node fails to delete the key as agreed (or maliciously retains it), what recourse does the user have? Is there any on-chain slashing, penalty, or cryptographic guarantee (e.g., threshold schemes where no single node can decrypt alone)? If the guarantee is purely “nodes are honest and will delete,” please state that honestly and discuss the trust assumptions.
Please revise and resubmit based on the feedback above. We will arrange a new round of review as soon as possible.
Best,
xingtian
On behalf of the Spark Program Committee
cc: @zz_tovarishch , @yixiu.ckbfans.bit , @Hanssen

recent_posts.content_text:
Hi @duongja ,
Thank you for your persistence and hard work. The committee has completed its final evaluation of the Dular project and believes that you have made sufficient effort and delivered commendable performance; therefore, the committee has approved the project’s completion. Additionally, the committee has reviewed the new content you published and recognizes its value.
However, since the completion application for the Dular project was submitted two months later than expected, the committee believes that you should formally explain the reasons for the delay of more than two months in your personal completion report and share your experience with the community based on the actual circumstances, thereby helping other community members better understand and assess the various issues that may arise during the development process.
I will publish the completion report for the Dular project as soon as possible.
Best，
xingtian
On behalf of the Spark Program Committee
cc： @zz_tovarishch , @Hanssen , @yixiu.ckbfans.bit
